reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: An acute idiopathic lower motor neuron facial palsy that involves the whole of one side of the face, including the forehead
Forehead sparing points instead to an upper motor neuron (central) lesion, because the upper face has bilateral cortical representation, and warrants a search for a stroke or other central cause
Onset is usually rapid over hours to a couple of days, and patients may report ipsilateral ear or postauricular pain preceding weakness
Associated features can include altered taste, hyperacusis, and reduced tear production depending on the level of the lesion along the facial nerve
Incomplete eye closure risks exposure keratopathy, so eye protection with lubrication and taping is an essential part of care
Early corticosteroid treatment improves the likelihood of complete recovery, and antiviral therapy is sometimes added in severe cases
Bilateral facial palsy or additional cranial nerve involvement suggests an alternative diagnosis and requires further investigation
A vesicular rash in the ear or palate indicates Ramsay Hunt syndrome from herpes zoster rather than Bell's palsy
reference.pathophysiology: Bell's palsy is an acute mononeuropathy of the facial (seventh cranial) nerve, widely attributed to inflammation and oedema of the nerve, often linked to reactivation of herpes simplex virus. Swelling of the nerve within the narrow bony facial canal causes compression, ischaemia, and demyelination, producing unilateral weakness of all facial muscles on the affected side. Depending on the segment involved, taste, lacrimation, and stapedius function may also be impaired.
additionalDifferentials: Ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke causing central facial weakness
Lyme disease, especially with bilateral palsy
Cerebellopontine angle or parotid tumour compressing the facial nerve
Otitis media, cholesteatoma, or skull base pathology; sarcoidosis
additionalInvestigations: Careful clinical examination to confirm the lower motor neuron pattern and exclude other cranial nerve involvement
Otoscopy and skin inspection for vesicles suggesting Ramsay Hunt syndrome
Serology for Lyme disease in endemic areas or with bilateral palsy
MRI of the brain and facial nerve when the presentation is atypical, progressive, or recurrent
Investigation for sarcoidosis or other systemic causes when clinically indicated
redFlags: Forehead-sparing weakness or other focal deficits suggesting a central cause such as stroke
Gradually progressive or recurrent weakness suggesting a compressive or neoplastic lesion
Bilateral facial palsy prompting evaluation for systemic disease
Failure of eye closure with corneal exposure risking sight-threatening keratopathy
reference.prognosis: Most patients with Bell's palsy recover well, and the majority regain normal or near-normal function, particularly with early corticosteroid treatment and when weakness is incomplete. A minority, especially those with complete paralysis, are left with residual weakness, synkinesis, or contracture. Recovery beginning within the first few weeks predicts a favourable outcome.
pitfalls: Missing a central cause by not checking for forehead involvement
Neglecting eye protection and allowing exposure keratopathy
Overlooking Ramsay Hunt syndrome or Lyme disease as specific, treatable causes
Failing to reassess a palsy that is progressive, recurrent, or slow to recover for an underlying structural lesion
management: Start oral corticosteroids (prednisolone) as early as possible after symptom onset to improve the likelihood of complete recovery
Add antiviral therapy such as aciclovir or valaciclovir alongside corticosteroids in severe or complete palsy
Protect the eye with lubricating drops and ointment, taping or patching it closed at night to prevent exposure keratopathy
Reassure that most patients recover well, and arrange follow-up to confirm recovery
Consider facial physiotherapy and neuromuscular retraining for slow or incomplete recovery, with attention to synkinesis
Treat Ramsay Hunt syndrome, if vesicles are found, with antivirals and corticosteroids
Refer for further evaluation and imaging if the palsy is atypical, progressive, recurrent, bilateral or fails to recover
